lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: This is the last night of Troy.

lines.speaker: ILOS
lines.text: They're gone! The Greeks are gone! Ten years, and they just sailed away!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: And they left us a giant wooden horse. Doesn't that seem strange to you?

lines.speaker: ILOS
lines.text: It's a gift to the gods, brother. Drink! We won!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: You are a Trojan soldier. You survived ten years of war. In six hours, your city will burn. To see how, go back ten years.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Troy. A rich city on the coast of Anatolia, guarding the sea road to the Black Sea. Today, its ruins lie in Turkey, near Çanakkale.

lines.speaker: DAD
lines.text: Hold the reins steady, son. Troy breeds the finest horses in the world.

lines.speaker: ILOS
lines.text: Did you see her at the harbor? They say she's the most beautiful woman alive.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: I saw a lot of Spartan gold. And a lot of guards.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Father, is it true? Prince Paris came back from Sparta with another man's wife?

lines.speaker: DAD
lines.text: Helen. Queen of Sparta. And her husband's brother is Agamemnon, the most powerful king in Greece.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: So what happens now?

lines.speaker: DAD
lines.text: Now? Now we sharpen our spears.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: A war? Over one woman?

lines.speaker: DAD
lines.text: Wars are never about one woman, son. Every ship that sails to the Black Sea passes our coast. The Greeks want what we have.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: A year later, you're on the wall at dawn.

lines.speaker: ILOS
lines.text: Gods. Look at the sea. How many ships are there?

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: I stopped counting at three hundred.

lines.speaker: ILOS
lines.text: Look! Prince Hector is coming down from the palace!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Homer lists more than a thousand ships. Probably far fewer. But to you, it looks like the whole world has come for Troy.

lines.speaker: HEC
lines.text: Trojans! To the beach! Push them back into the sea!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: A prophecy said the first Greek to step onto Trojan soil would die. He jumps anyway. He dies at once.

lines.speaker: ILOS
lines.text: Ha! Who wants to be second?

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Thousands do. The Greeks take the beach.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: But they can't take the city. So they build a camp on the shore, and they stay. Year after year.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Nine years, Ilos. I was sixteen when this started.

lines.speaker: ILOS
lines.text: And now you're old and ugly. Pass the bread.

lines.speaker: ILOS
lines.text: My uncle says the Greeks are so hungry, they're eating their own horses.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Your uncle also says he once wrestled a lion.

lines.speaker: ILOS
lines.text: A small lion. It still counts.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Father, why don't they just attack the walls?

lines.speaker: DAD
lines.text: Look at them. The old songs say Poseidon himself built these walls.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Did he?

lines.speaker: DAD
lines.text: No. But the walls are real. And no ladder in Greece is tall enough.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: A full bronze armor costs as much as a farm. Most men fight with a spear, a shield of wood and leather, and a lot of hope.

lines.speaker: DAD
lines.text: Shield high. And never, ever break the line. A line of shields is a wall. A man alone is just a target.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Yes, Father. Never break the line.

lines.speaker: SCOUT
lines.text: News from the Greek camp! Achilles has quarreled with King Agamemnon!

lines.speaker: ILOS
lines.text: Achilles? Their best fighter?

lines.speaker: SCOUT
lines.text: He's sitting in his tent. He swears he won't fight for them anymore.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: What did they fight about?

lines.speaker: SCOUT
lines.text: A captive girl named Briseis. Agamemnon took her from him, so Achilles took himself out of the war.

lines.speaker: HEC
lines.text: Then tomorrow we attack. We will burn their ships!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: If their ships burn, they can never go home.

lines.speaker: ILOS
lines.text: Then they'll fight like wolves in a corner. Sleep well, brother.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: This is what Homer's Iliad is really about: the anger of Achilles. And for the first time in nine years, Troy is winning.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Dawn. The gates open, and thousands of Trojans pour onto the plain. You're in the front line.

lines.speaker: HEC
lines.text: Trojans! Today we fight for our wives, our children, and the walls of our fathers! Forward!

lines.speaker: ILOS
lines.text: Shields up! Stay together! Whatever happens, stay next to me!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Chariots thunder past. Arrows hiss overhead. Then the two armies crash together.

lines.speaker: ILOS
lines.text: Chariot! Get down!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Ilos! On your left!

lines.speaker: ILOS
lines.text: I see him! Push! Push!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Hold the line! Don't break the line!

lines.speaker: HEC
lines.text: Fire! Bring fire to the ships!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The first Greek ship goes up in flames. And then, out of the smoke, a warrior in shining armor charges straight at you.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Achilles! It's Achilles!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: It isn't. It's his best friend, Patroclus, wearing his armor. Hector cuts him down. And now, Achilles will come for revenge.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Ilos! Are you hurt?

lines.speaker: ILOS
lines.text: Just a scratch. Bronze is cheaper than skin.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: That evening, you're guarding the gate when Hector stops to say goodbye to his wife.

lines.speaker: AND
lines.text: Hector, please. Stay inside the walls. If you die, what happens to us?

lines.speaker: HEC
lines.text: If I hide, I could never look a Trojan in the eye again. I have to fight.

lines.speaker: AND
lines.text: Then come back to us.

lines.speaker: HEC
lines.text: I will try. That is all a soldier can promise.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: He reaches for his baby son. The child screams, terrified of the horsehair crest on his helmet. Hector laughs, takes it off, and kisses him.

lines.speaker: HEC
lines.text: One day, may they say of you: he is even braver than his father.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The next day, Achilles returns. Every Trojan runs for the gates. Except one.

lines.speaker: ILOS
lines.text: Hector! Get inside! Hector!

lines.speaker: ACH
lines.text: Hector! Turn and face me!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Achilles chases him around the walls three times. Then it's over.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Hector is dead. Who will protect Troy now?

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: That night, old King Priam walks alone into the enemy camp, and kneels before Achilles.

lines.speaker: PRI
lines.text: Remember your own father, Achilles. I have done what no man has done. I have kissed the hands of the man who killed my son.

lines.speaker: ACH
lines.text: Get up, old man. Take him home.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The Iliad ends right here, with Hector's funeral. Not with the fall of Troy.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Months later, you wake up to silence. The Greek camp is empty. And on the beach stands a giant wooden horse.

lines.speaker: ILOS
lines.text: They've given up! It's an offering. We should take it to the temple!

lines.speaker: LAO
lines.text: Are you mad? Burn it! I fear the Greeks, even when they bring gifts!

lines.speaker: SIN
lines.text: Wait! I am Sinon. The Greeks left me behind. The horse is an offering to Athena. They built it huge, so you could never take it into your city, because if you did, Troy could never fall.

lines.speaker: CAS
lines.text: Fire! I see fire and blood! Troy is burning!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: That's Princess Cassandra. The gods cursed her. She always tells the truth, and nobody ever believes her.

lines.speaker: ILOS
lines.text: She says that about everything.

lines.speaker: ILOS
lines.text: Come on, grab a rope! Pull!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The horse is too big for the gate. So the Trojans break open their own wall to bring it in.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: We just broke our own wall, for a horse.

lines.speaker: ILOS
lines.text: Relax! Tonight, we celebrate!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Back to tonight. Midnight. While Troy sleeps, a hidden door opens in the belly of the horse.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Ilos. Ilos, wake up! Do you hear that?

lines.speaker: ILOS
lines.text: The gates! Someone has opened the gates!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Get your shield! Where's your spear?

lines.speaker: ILOS
lines.text: Go! Find my mother! I'll hold them here!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The Greek fleet was hiding behind the island of Tenedos. Now the whole army is inside the walls.

lines.speaker: AEN
lines.text: Trojan! This way! The city is lost. Save who you can!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Ilos! Ilos, come on!

lines.speaker: ILOS
lines.text: Go! Remember me, brother!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: You follow Prince Aeneas through the smoke. He carries his old father on his back.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Where are we going?

lines.speaker: AEN
lines.text: Wherever the sea takes us. As long as we live, Troy lives.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Roman legend says Aeneas sailed west to Italy, and his descendants founded Rome.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: So, was any of it real?

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: In eighteen seventy-one, Heinrich Schliemann dug into a hill called Hisarlık, near Çanakkale. He found not one city, but nine, built on top of each other.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Nine Troys? Which one was mine?

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: One of them burned around eleven eighty BC. Archaeologists found signs of fire, and arrowheads and sling stones in its streets.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: And in Hittite archives, there are letters about a kingdom called Wilusa, which sounds a lot like Ilios, Homer's name for Troy. One of its kings was called Alaksandu.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Alaksandu. Alexandros. That's Paris's other name!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: And the horse?

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The horse isn't in the Iliad at all. Some historians think it's a memory of a siege engine. Or of an earthquake: Poseidon was the god of both horses and earthquakes.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: So the war might have been real?

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The city was real. And it burned. The rest, historians are still arguing about.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: So, if you'd been standing in that square, looking up at the horse, would you have pulled it inside? Tell me in the comments.
